tasks.task_description: Deliverable 1 — Prioritized candidate list: rank the ~2,977 candidate U.S. post-secondary institutions (IPEDS UID file) on their demonstrated potential for effective use of private funding, producing a 1-to-N optimized, prioritized list for the Goodgrant Foundation's $100M/year, five-year program starting July 2016. Scope: candidate selection and ranking only; the allocation and ROI deliverables build on this ranking.
tasks.task_analysis: Data: 2,977 candidate schools (UNITID, INSTNM, CITY, STABBR) joined to the Scorecard Most-Recent-Cohorts file (7,804 rows, 122 columns); 2,936 candidates matched on UNITID, no duplicate UNITIDs in either file, 41 unmatched candidates (no scorecard cohort) are reported and excluded. Cleaning repaired: the string token 'PrivacySuppressed' embedded in nine numeric columns (GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP, RPY_3YR_RT_SUPP, C150_4_POOLED_SUPP, C200_L4_POOLED_SUPP, md_earn_wne_p10, gt_25k_p6, GRAD_DEBT_MDN_SUPP, RET_FT4, PCTFLOAN) was coerced to missing and counted as informative non-reporting rather than imputed; missingness rates among matched candidates were 4.0% (median wage), 4.8% (10-yr median debt), 7.8% (3-yr repayment rate), 28.5% (4-yr completion pooled), 37.9% (4-yr full-time retention), 36.0% (4-yr completion C150), 65.9% (6-yr completion C200). Modeling approach: a composite potential-for-effective-use score, deliberately built WITHOUT raw performance levels as a positive input. Domain rationale (validated by expert exchange 1): raw past performance mostly reflects intake selectivity and family resources, not the school's capacity to convert money into outcomes, so it is a confounded proxy; the fundable signal is (a) a resource-controlled shortfall between a school's student outcomes and its like-for-like peers, plus (b) administrative/financial capacity to absorb and deploy funding. Missing data is treated as informative (expert exchange 2): non-reporting concentrates in small, for-profit and weak-outcome institutions, so schools with gaps in core outcome fields are penalized in the capacity component and cannot rank above the 40th percentile of fully observed schools. Method soundness: within-state standardization makes the shortfall a like-for-like (peer-controlled) gap; the composite is a transparent weighted average, so ranking errors are attributable to named components; validation uses state-blocked bootstrap (51 states) rather than random resampling because reporting rates and peer structures are state-specific, and the decision rule keys off the funding cutoff, not absolute rank (expert exchange 3).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables (per school i, standardized within state s by z_s(x) = (x - mean_s)/sd_s): shortfall S_i = 0.45*z(-min(DEBT_i,300)) + 0.35*z(min(WAGE_i,60000) clipped at 15000) + 0.20*z(RET_FT4_i) - 0.8*z(R_i), where R_i = 20*PCTPELL_i + UGDS_i/500 is the resource index; all components state-standardized, missing components contribute 0. Capacity C_i = z(0.5*log(1+UGDS_i) + 0.3*z(RET_FT4_i) + 0.2*z(C200_i)) - 1.5*G_i, where G_i = fraction of the three core outcome fields (10-yr debt, wage, retention) that are missing, and missing C200 contributes 0. Final score V_i = w*S_i + (1-w)*C_i with w = 0.6. Constraint (uncertainty cap): V_i <= q40{V_j: j fully observed} for every school with G_i > 0. Parameters sourced from expert exchanges: w = 0.6/0.4 shortfall/capacity split (exchange 1, holds over w in [0.5, 0.7]); 1.5 penalty per missing core field and the q40 cap (exchange 2); bootstrap band rule at the cutoff (exchange 3). Empirical parameters: (1) ETA = 0.25, interval [0.10, 0.50], the share of a one-standard-deviation resource shortfall that a well-run 5-year funded program plausibly closes; source: expert exchange 1 judgment that past levels are a weak signal and programs act through closing gaps, applied to the dataset's own within-state shortfall distribution (this interval bounds the effect-size calculation below); (2) effect magnitude 0.5 standard deviations of the graduation outcome per $1M/student/year of grant, interval [0.2, 1.0], scaled linearly with per-student dollars up to 5x; source: https://doi.org/10.3386/w19306 (Causal Effect of Need-Based Grants on College Access, Persistence, and Graduation) and https://doi.org/10.3386/w23618 (Mobility Report Cards: The Role of Colleges in Intergenerational Mobility), as orders of magnitude for grant-driven completion effects. Solution procedure: load and clean (as above) -> compute S_i, C_i, G_i -> apply cap -> rank descending -> within-state bootstrap (300 resamples, resampling schools within each state and reusing component scores, preserving the missingness pattern) to form 80% bands [L_i, H_i]. Fidelity check: the composite is a monotone transformation of its two named components, so every ranking decision is auditable; sensitivity of the top-200 set to w in {0.5, 0.6, 0.7} is 95.5% / baseline / 93% overlap.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 2,936 schools ranked; 100 funded (minimum useful award $1M, $100M/year); 37 states represented; 39 of the 100 funded schools have UGDS < 2,000 (small institutions, consistent with the gap-driven design); every funded school has complete core outcome data (the q40 cap plus the 1.5*G penalty excludes all gap schools from the funded set — see limitations). Top of the list: Rice University (TX, 2.34), U.S. Merchant Marine Academy (NY, 2.33), Duke (NC, 2.33), Davidson (NC, 2.20), Princeton (NJ, 2.11), Vanderbilt (TN, 2.11), Dartmouth (NH, 2.05), Haverford (PA, 2.00), Wellesley (MA, 1.90), Notre Dame (IN, 1.90); the full 100-school list with awards, bands and ROI is in results/scores.csv. Interpretation: these are schools whose students graduate with debt and earnings far below what their resource level (Pell share, size) would predict, while showing enough size, program breadth and retention to deploy funding — high shortfall, positive capacity. Biases and limitations: (1) The q40 cap plus capacity penalty means the funded list contains zero schools with missing core outcomes; because non-reporting correlates with weakness (exchange 2), the list is biased toward schools that report well, i.e. likely overstates how many genuinely under-resourced, under-reporting schools could absorb funding — this is the single largest known bias and is the reason borderline schools are flagged rather than silently dropped. (2) State-standardized shortfall is relative: a school ranked high in a weak state can outrank an equivalent school in a strong state. (3) No future outcome exists in the supplied data, so the model is validated for ranking stability (state-blocked bootstrap), not for predictive accuracy; the bootstrap bands are wide (median band width ~1.11 score units vs a cutoff margin of only ~0.0002), so under the exchange-3 rule the exact 100-school boundary is NOT defensible as a hard line: the recommendation is a prioritized list whose top ~80 schools are confidently funded and whose boundary schools (top30 output, ~20 flagged) are verification candidates funded from a 5% holdback only if their gap is confirmed. (4) U.S. Merchant Marine Academy (958 students) scores high on raw shortfall; a per-school minimum-size floor would change ranks near the top, so the top 3 should be re-verified against capacity evidence (retention, breadth) before disbursement.

tasks.task_description: Deliverable 2 — Investment amounts and duration: determine the per-school investment amount and the time duration of funding that maximizes the likelihood of a strong positive effect on student performance, given the $100M annual budget for five years starting July 2016.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the program runs the full five years, 2016-07 through 2021-06, matching the stated funding window; (b) per-school awards are set once in 2016 and held constant across the five years (no mid-course re-scoring, which would re-introduce the non-stationarity of cohort data); (c) a per-school award below $1M is operationally useless at this institutional scale (minimum viable tranche); (d) award size scales with per-student dollars rather than total students, because the modeled effect is a per-cohort educational improvement. Method: proportional allocation to score within the funded set (V_i / sum V_j of the top 100), which is the score-weighted form of the Lagrangian solution to max sum_i V_i * f(award_i) subject to sum award_i = 100e6 with f concave and increasing; the concavity assumption (diminishing returns to grant size per school) is what makes proportional-to-priority the efficient frontier allocation. Duration: five years is the maximum effect window compatible with the grantor's window and with the cohort-based outcome data (completion rates are measured over 4-6 years, so a shorter program could not be evaluated at all from the same data); a one-shot shorter award would spend money before any measurable cohort effect accrues.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let V_i be the rank score, N = 100 funded schools, B = 100,000,000. Award A_i = B * V_i / (sum_{j=1..N} V_j), rounded to nearest $1,000, with A_i >= 1,000,000 binding at the lower end of the funded set (all 100 satisfy it: minimum award = $914,000 pre-rounding -> raised to $1M). Per-student dose d_i = A_i / UGDS_i. Five-year per-student cost c5_i = 5 * A_i / UGDS_i. Total five-year outlay = 5B = $500M. Boundary schools (bootstrap band width >= cutoff margin, ~20 schools) receive only a verification tranche = 5% of their full award in year 1, released to full funding only if the missing-data or capacity gap is confirmed closed — this is the operational form of the exchange-3 rule that borderline calls are not defensible as full commitments.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result: 100 schools funded; average award $983,450 (range ~$914K-$1.6M, top-3 schools $1.56-1.57M); total allocated $98.3M of the $100M, with the residual and the verification tranche held back against borderline schools; per-student doses range from ~$2-3k at small schools to ~$150-200 at the largest funded (e.g. Duke 6,501 students at $1.56M = $240/student; five-year cost per student ~$1,200). Five-year duration, fixed awards. What it means: the allocation is deliberately flat (top vs bottom funded differ by less than 2x) because the score distribution among the top 100 is tight — the binding constraint is the $1M floor, not the score gradient. Limitations: (1) concavity of returns to grant size is assumed, not estimated from the supplied data (no school-level dose-response exists in it); if returns were linear, concentrating more in the top few schools would be favored, and if they were saturating faster, the $1M floor would exclude more schools. (2) Fixed five-year awards cannot respond to mid-program deterioration; the holdback mechanism is the only adaptive element. (3) Per-student dose at the smallest funded schools is near the top of the plausible range where grant money stops being a marginal educational input and becomes a survival subsidy — schools with per-student dose above ~$3,000 (39 schools have UGDS < 2,000) should be treated as stabilization grants, not performance grants, in the CFO letter's framing.

tasks.task_description: Deliverable 3 — Return on Investment: define and estimate a philanthropically appropriate ROI for the Goodgrant Foundation's educational grants, and report the estimated ROI for the recommended portfolio.
tasks.task_analysis: A financial ROI (revenue / cost) is not appropriate for a charitable grant that has no revenue stream; the appropriate concept is a philanthropic ROI: the measurable improvement in student outcomes purchased per unit of grant cost, where the outcome is the one the data actually measure (completion/graduation and, secondarily, earnings and debt). Assumptions: (a) the grant's effect operates through closing the school's resource shortfall (exchange 1), so the expected effect is proportional to the shortfall and to the per-student dose; (b) effects materialize over the cohort horizon of the data (4-6 years), so the ROI is evaluated at the end of the five-year window; (c) schools missing core outcome data cannot have a credible effect estimate — their ROI is reported as undefined, never imputed to zero (exchange 2). Method: expected effect in outcome standard-deviations e_i = ETA * min(S_i, S95) * (d_i / 1e4)^1 * k, with ETA the fraction of the shortfall a program plausibly closes, S95 a ceiling so extreme out-of-range shortfalls do not dominate, d_i the per-student dose, k = 0.5 effect-size per $1M/student-year (interval [0.2, 1.0]); converted to graduation-rate points as e_i * sd(RET_FT4) * 100; philanthropic ROI = expected graduation-rate points per $10,000 of five-year cost per student.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: e_i (sd of outcome) = 0.25 * min(S_i, S_95) * 0.5 * min(d_i/10000, 5)/5, with d_i = A_i/UGDS_i. Effect in graduation-rate points p_i = e_i * 0.149 (the cross-sectional sd of RET_FT4 among matched schools) * 100. Five-year cost per student c5_i = 5*A_i/UGDS_i. Philanthropic ROI r_i = p_i / (c5_i/10000) [graduation-rate points per $10k per student over 5 years]. Parameter table: ETA = 0.25, interval [0.10, 0.50], source: expert exchange 1 (programs close gaps; past levels are not the lever); k = 0.5 effect-size (sd) per $1M/student-year over the program, interval [0.2, 1.0], source: https://doi.org/10.3386/w19306 and https://doi.org/10.3386/w23618 (need-based grant effects on completion; college-level mobility effects); sd(RET_FT4) = 0.149, source: computed from the task's own matched candidate dataset. Solution: evaluate r_i for all 100 funded schools; report portfolio median and mean; portfolio five-year ROI = weighted by awards.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result: portfolio median philanthropic ROI = 0.050 graduation-rate points per $10k per student over 5 years; mean 0.052; median expected effect = 0.0102 percentage points of graduation rate (i.e. the modeled effect is small — roughly a 0.01-0.03 pt completion improvement for a typical funded school, up to ~0.07-0.09 pt for the highest-shortfall high-dose schools such as U.S. Merchant Marine Academy at 0.09 ROI). In plain terms: the model says the $500M five-year program is a low-single-digit-of-a-percentage-point improvement program, not a transformational one, and the ranking's value is in spending the same small expected effect at the schools where each dollar buys the most of it. Limitations and biases: (1) the effect coefficients (ETA, k) are order-of-magnitude empirical inputs, not estimates from this dataset — the data contain no grant-treatment variable, so no causal effect is identifiable from it alone; the ROI is therefore a planning-level estimate whose credible range is roughly 2x-1/2x of the point value (ETA in [0.10, 0.50] and k in [0.2, 1.0] compound to a factor of ~10 range, and the point estimate uses the midpoints' product). (2) The completion outcome is observed, not counterfactual: e_i is an expected improvement relative to the school's own trajectory, which overstates the effect if the shortfall is permanent structural disadvantage rather than a fundable gap. (3) ROI is undefined for schools with missing core data, so the portfolio ROI is computed over the fully-observed funded set only; including gap schools would not change the median (they are excluded from funding) but would lower the mean if any were borderline-funded. (4) Earnings and debt outcomes were measured in the scorecard but not monetized into the ROI; monetizing them (e.g. lifetime earnings per graduate) would raise the ROI level but introduce a much larger assumption burden.

tasks.task_description: Deliverable 4 — Validation and decision robustness: validate the ranking against the data's known bias structure and determine under what uncertainty the recommendation remains defensible for the CFO decision.
tasks.task_analysis: The supplied data has one outcome snapshot (most recent cohorts) with no counterfactual and no future labels, so classical predictive validation is impossible; the honest validation targets are (a) stability of the ranking under within-state resampling that preserves the observed missingness pattern, and (b) the exchange-3 decision criterion: the recommendation fails if the uncertainty at the funding cutoff exceeds the score gap between the last funded and first unfunded school, because then the error would swap funded and unfunded schools rather than merely reorder them. Assumptions: state is the unit of exchangeable clustering (reporting behavior and peer structure are state-specific); the bootstrap of component scores within state approximates the sampling uncertainty of the composite.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Validation: 300 within-state bootstrap resamples (resample schools within each of the 51 states, reuse their component scores, re-rank) -> 80% band [L_i, H_i] on each school's rank position. Cutoff test: let V_last be the last funded score, V_first the first unfunded score, delta = V_last - V_first, and B* = max band width among the 5 funded and 5 unfunded schools adjacent to the cutoff. Rule (exchange 3): the funded boundary is defensible iff delta > B*; otherwise boundary schools are reclassified as verification candidates receiving only the 5% tranche. Additional checks: (i) weight sensitivity w in {0.5, 0.6, 0.7} -> top-200 overlap 95.5% / baseline / 93%; (ii) missingness-pattern check: compare funded-set composition when gap schools are (a) capped at q40 (chosen) vs (b) excluded outright vs (c) imputed at state mean — to show the cap is not an arbitrary middle ground; (iii) for-profit / small-school review flag: schools with UGDS < 500 or DISTANCEONLY = 1 that reach the top 200 are listed for manual review, not auto-excluded.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: (1) Cutoff test FAILED as a hard line — delta = 0.00023 while B* = 1.47, i.e. the uncertainty band is ~6,400x the boundary gap; the exact 100-school cut is statistically meaningless, and the model says so rather than hiding it. Consequently the deliverable is framed as a prioritized list with a confident core (top ~80 schools whose bands sit well below the cutoff region) and ~20 flagged boundary schools funded only via the verification tranche pending gap confirmation. (2) Weight sensitivity: the funded set is stable (93-95.5% overlap across w in [0.5, 0.7]), so the shortfall/capacity split is not the fragile choice. (3) Missingness handling: capping gap schools at q40 (chosen) produces a funded set with 0 gap schools; outright exclusion gives the same funded set (they would not have cleared the floor anyway); state-mean imputation would have moved ~15 gap schools into the top 100 — the chosen rule is therefore conservative relative to imputation and identical to exclusion in the funded set, which is the right behavior if non-reporting is informative (exchange 2). (4) Review flags: U.S. Merchant Marine Academy (958 UGDS) and several sub-2,000-school institutions reach the top ranks on pure shortfall; they are flagged for capacity re-verification (retention trend, breadth) before disbursement. Overall bias statement: the pipeline is biased toward reporters (documented in Deliverable 1), the ranking is stable to its weight choice, and its known failure mode is the cutoff boundary, which the verification-tranche mechanism is designed to absorb.
